Baby & Child

Cryptophthalmos: types, vision and specialist treatment

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Cryptophthalmos is a rare condition present at birth in which normal eyelid separation and the surface of the eye have not developed properly. Skin may cover all or part of an eye. Early specialist assessment checks the eye itself, protects any visual potential and looks for associated health needs.

What cryptophthalmos means

The condition was described in the medical literature in the nineteenth century. Instead of normal separated eyelids, skin may continue from the forehead toward the cheek and adhere to the eye’s surface. Eyebrows or eyelashes may be missing. The eye underneath can be small, severely underdeveloped, absent or occasionally more normally formed; not every child has the same anatomy.

One or both eyes can be affected, and the two sides can differ. The three conventional terms (complete, incomplete and abortive) describe the visible arrangement of skin and eyelids. They help plan assessment, but do not alone establish vision, associated conditions or the best operation.

Complete cryptophthalmos

In the complete form, continuous skin covers the eye region from forehead to cheek, without a normal eyelid opening. Eyelashes and eyebrows may be absent, and normal spaces around the eye may not have formed. The globe and cornea underneath are often substantially abnormal.

Vision is frequently very limited, but “complete” must not automatically be translated as absolutely no visual potential. A published surgical series included a rare complete case with hand-movement vision after reconstruction. This is not a promise of recovery: individual examination and imaging are needed, and reconstructing eyelids cannot create a missing or nonfunctioning eye.

Incomplete and abortive forms

In incomplete cryptophthalmos, some eyelid structures or an opening remain, while skin covers another part of the eye region. The amount of covering and the globe’s development vary. Partial covering does not necessarily mean only a minor problem or predict useful sight.

The abortive form, also called congenital symblepharon, usually involves deficient upper eyelid tissue adhering to the upper eye surface, with an abnormal upper conjunctival recess or fornix. The lower eyelid may be better formed. Here “abortive” is an anatomical term, not a reference to pregnancy termination. Exposed cornea can dry or become damaged, so protecting the eye surface may be urgent.

Isolated findings and Fraser syndrome

Cryptophthalmos can occur on its own or as part of a wider condition. A key association is Fraser syndrome, which can also involve skin joining fingers or toes, kidney or urinary-tract differences, genital differences and airway abnormalities. Not every affected child has all these findings. Fraser syndrome is distinct from Fryns syndrome; the names are not interchangeable.

Assessment therefore extends beyond the eyelids. A pediatric team may arrange kidney evaluation, airway and feeding assessment, hearing checks and genetics review according to the findings. Breathing or feeding safety takes priority over elective reconstruction. Associated airway or kidney problems can be serious, but the eye’s appearance alone cannot predict survival or development.

What genetics can and cannot explain

Fraser syndrome can be caused by pathogenic variants in FRAS1, FREM2 or GRIP1 and is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern: both copies of the relevant gene are affected. Parents carrying one altered copy commonly have no symptoms. If both parents are confirmed carriers for the same recessive condition, the chance of an affected child is 25% in each pregnancy; this figure must not be applied automatically to every isolated eyelid finding.

The cause or inheritance of an individual child’s cryptophthalmos may remain uncertain. Related parents can have a higher chance of sharing a recessive variant, but that relationship is neither required nor a sufficient explanation. A genetics professional can interpret testing, family history and future-pregnancy options. This condition is not evidence of ordinary parental actions causing harm.

Diagnosis before and after birth

Ultrasound during pregnancy sometimes identifies the eye or associated organ differences, but a normal scan cannot exclude every case. When a family’s causative variants are known, fetal-medicine and genetics teams can discuss appropriate diagnostic testing and its limits. A routine screening result should not be treated as a definitive diagnosis or exclusion of this rare condition.

After birth, pediatric ophthalmology and reconstructive eye specialists examine eyelids, the cornea, the globe and potential vision, using imaging when appropriate. The team also evaluates associated health needs. Ask what is known, what remains uncertain, whether the surface is exposed, and which findings would change the timing or goal of treatment.

Protecting the eye and planning surgery

Treatment depends on the eye’s structure, visual potential, exposure and the child’s overall health. Clinician-prescribed lubrication or other protection may be needed; early surgery can be important when exposed cornea is at risk. Do not try to separate attached skin or eyelids, force an opening or use unprescribed drops. Timing is individualized rather than fixed for every child.

Reconstruction may create or improve eyelids, the upper fornix and a protective eye surface using specialist techniques and sometimes grafts. Some children need staged procedures; adhesions can recur. When useful vision is not possible, care may focus on comfort, protection and socket development, sometimes with a conformer or prosthesis. Appearance, closure and vision are different outcomes: surgery cannot guarantee normal sight.

Follow-up, support and warning signs

Keep the ophthalmology and pediatric follow-up plan, including eye-surface care, vision or low-vision support and any hearing, feeding or developmental services needed. Ask for written instructions about medicines, appointments and who to contact. New eye redness, pain, discharge, cloudiness or worsening exposure needs prompt specialist advice, not waiting for the next routine visit.

Seek emergency help for difficult or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or skin, unusually pale or blotchy skin, skin that feels cold or damp (clammy), fainting or loss of consciousness, or a baby who is floppy, unresponsive or difficult to wake. A temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby under 3 months needs immediate medical help. In any baby or child, a temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours also needs immediate medical help. Poor feeding or other new concerns also need urgent advice; do not wait for all warning signs to appear.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current specialist descriptions distinguish complete, incomplete and abortive forms, while assessing the underlying globe and cornea separately.

Fraser syndrome assessment includes associated organ needs and individualized genetic counselling. Its recessive inheritance should not be assumed for every isolated eyelid finding.

Published reconstruction series are small and largely retrospective. Protecting visual potential and improving eyelid function are important goals, but surgery and study percentages cannot guarantee an individual outcome.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize appointments, prescribed eye care, feeding observations and questions for the specialist team. It cannot assess vision, diagnose a syndrome or decide surgical timing. New eye or general warning signs override an app reminder or routine appointment.

When to seek help

Do not force an eyelid opening or use unprescribed eye treatment. Seek prompt eye-specialist advice for new pain, redness, cloudiness, discharge or worsening exposure. Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusually pale or blotchy skin, skin that feels cold or damp (clammy), fainting or loss of consciousness, or a floppy, unresponsive or hard-to-wake baby needs emergency help. A temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby under 3 months needs immediate medical help. In any baby or child, a temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours also needs immediate medical help.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Cryptophthalmos can affect one or both eyes; the type alone does not predict vision.
  • Fraser syndrome is an important association, distinct from Fryns syndrome; associated airway and kidney needs matter.
  • Protecting exposed cornea may be urgent. Reconstruction is individualized and cannot guarantee normal sight.
  • Continue coordinated eye and pediatric follow-up, with immediate help for breathing or consciousness problems.

Frequently asked questions

What causes cryptophthalmos?

It reflects abnormal development of the eyelids and eye surface before birth. It may be isolated or part of a condition such as Fraser syndrome. Genetics can sometimes identify a cause, but not every case has the same inheritance or a clear explanation.

Can it be diagnosed during pregnancy?

Sometimes ultrasound shows eye or associated organ differences, but it can miss cases. If a family’s causative variants are known, specialist diagnostic options can be discussed. A normal routine screening scan does not exclude every case.

How is it treated?

Specialists assess the globe, cornea, visual potential and overall health. Treatment may include surface protection and individualized reconstruction of eyelids or surrounding spaces. Some children need staged operations, comfort or socket care and visual support. Normal vision cannot be promised.

What does abortive cryptophthalmos mean?

It is a partial anatomical form, also called congenital symblepharon, in which abnormal upper eyelid tissue adheres to the upper eye surface. The term does not mean pregnancy termination. Corneal exposure can threaten remaining vision and needs specialist assessment.

Does the complete form always mean no vision?

Vision is often severely limited, but rare exceptions have been reported. The condition of the eye underneath matters. An individual specialist assessment is more useful than an absolute prediction from the label; reconstruction cannot restore a missing or nonfunctioning eye.

Is the chance in another pregnancy always 25%?

No. That figure applies when both parents are confirmed carriers for the same autosomal recessive condition. Isolated cryptophthalmos should not automatically be assigned that risk. Genetics counselling can address the particular diagnosis and family.

Must every baby have immediate reconstruction?

No single schedule suits every case. Exposed or threatened cornea may need early protection or surgery, while other procedures can be planned around visual potential, anatomy and overall health. Breathing and feeding safety take priority.

When should we seek urgent help?

Seek emergency help for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusually pale or blotchy skin, skin that feels cold or damp (clammy), fainting or loss of consciousness, or a floppy, unresponsive or hard-to-wake baby. A temperature of 38°C or higher in a baby under 3 months needs immediate medical help. In any baby or child, a temperature below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours also needs immediate medical help. New eye pain, redness, cloudiness, discharge or exposure needs prompt specialist advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
